title: Demand-aware pool throttling for progressive version rollouts
creator: Asha Patel
description: Problem: Upgrading dedicated GPU pools currently relies on large drain waves that cause transient capacity cliffs and unexpected autoscaler churn. This increases token latency for tail customers and forces conservative rollout windows. Goal: implement a demand-aware throttling layer that coordinates pool drains with autoscaler signals and request routing policies so we can do progressive version rollouts with minimal customer impact. This ticket covers the control-plane orchestration changes, rollout policy DSL, and the runtime handshake for per-pool throttling tokens.
design_notes: Introduce a throttling controller that emits a per-pool drain token with three phases: prepare, drain, and release.
Controller watches autoscaler metrics (pool_target_utilization, pending_queue_length) and only advances phase when safety invariants hold for a configurable observation window.

When entering 'prepare', controller reduces scheduling of new allocation to the pool by toggling a pool-level weight in the router; when entering 'drain', graceful eviction begins with prioritized eviction of noncritical workloads.
Routing layer will accept an optional 'throttle-respect' flag; host routing will divert a configurable percentage of traffic to fallback pools during drain phases.
Safety invariant examples: global free capacity >= min_capacity_buffer AND estimated spillover latency < latency_threshold for 5 consecutive minutes.
Design must support mixed-architecture pools (A100 + H100) and be compatible with Dedicated autoscaling policies and RBAC for private deployments.
rollout_plan: Phase 0 (lab): deploy controller to staging, run synthetic load tests with scripted drains to validate invariants.
Phase 1 (canary): enable throttling on a single low-traffic pool; collect impact metrics for 48 hours and confirm zero >2s latency regressions for P99.
Phase 2 (regional rollout): enable on 3 pools in different regions with gradual throttle percentages (10% -> 40% -> 100%) over 6 hours each.
Phase 3 (global): enable default 'throttle-respect' routing flag and use for all dedicated pool upgrades; monitor for 72 hours and enable automated fallback if spillover>5%.
Rollback: controller can abort and immediately release drain tokens if spillover breaches critical thresholds.
acceptance_criteria: Controller deployed and can move pools through prepare/drain/release via API and CLI.
Routing honors throttle flags and can divert configured percentages of traffic to fallback pools without service interruption.
Automated safety checks prevent advancing phases when estimated capacity impact would exceed thresholds.
Observability: new dashboard with per-pool drain state, spillover rate, P50/P95/P99 latency, and autoscaler decision logs.
Successful canary: no more than 0.5% increase in 99th-percentile token latency for affected customers during canary windows.
